definition: A smear frame (an artificial motion-blur pose bridging a fast action) can be built by one of three named construction methods: DOUBLES (drawing discrete duplicate copies of the moving object at successive past positions within the same frame, like a timing chart made visible), STREAK/BLUR (a single flowing, elongated line shape tracing and exaggerating the path of motion with no discrete copies), or BOTH combined (doubles overlaid with connecting streak lines) — the source's own stated preference and 'most natural-looking' of the three.
purpose: Give the animator interchangeable construction techniques for the same underlying smear-frame goal (implying long-exposure motion blur) rather than one fixed drawing method, with a stated ranking of which combination reads best.
visible_effect: Either several distinct, separated silhouette copies of the moving object trailing its current position (doubles); or a single continuous flowing/streaking line shape connecting the object's start and current position with no discrete copies (blur); or both layered together.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Reads as one continuous fast motion despite being represented by a sparse set of drawn frames, by supplying the visual information a real long-exposure photograph would have captured; the combined method is reported as the most convincing of the three.
physical_interpretation: A drawn simulation of long-exposure photography: the source frames it explicitly via a camera/shutter/sensor analogy — the longer a shutter stays open, the more of the object's path is visibly exposed at once — and states that smear density along the path was itself taken from filmed reference footage, not invented freehand.
use_cases: a fast swing or strike where filmed reference shows how blur density should be distributed along the motion path
a beginner-facing explicit menu of three named options (doubles / blur / both) rather than one undifferentiated 'draw a smear' instruction
a fast action animated on ones, where the source states smears read best at that frame rate specifically
non_use_cases: smearing a slow or already well-spaced action, where no motion-blur bridging problem exists to solve
animating the smear on twos or another lower frame rate, which the source says reads worse than on ones
drawing smear density uniformly along the whole path when reference footage would show it concentrated near the impact instead
interactions: motion_smear_readability (W01) — that entry names the general technique and Cadence's inability to represent it (no mesh deformation); this entry adds the specific CONSTRUCTION vocabulary (doubles vs. streak vs. both) and a stated best-practice ranking that entry does not itself give

multiples_vs_smear_for_differently_weighted_fast_motion (W06-57) — that entry's 'multiples' (discrete offset copies read as heavier/slower than a smear) appears to be the same visual mechanism as this video's 'doubles', but the two sources frame it differently: W06-57 treats multiples and a smear as ALTERNATIVE style choices for different weight readings, while this video treats doubles and streak-blur as COMBINABLE sub-techniques within one smear with no weight distinction stated — an open terminology/framing overlap worth reconciling at merge time, not resolved here

peak_spacing_immediately_before_impact (W04-34) — a related but distinct impact-proximity gradient: that entry is about keyframe SPACING/velocity increasing into contact, this entry is about smear-drawing DENSITY (how many blur/double marks) increasing into contact — plausibly two visible symptoms of the same reference-informed acceleration, but neither source measured both at once

prep_smear_slowdown_three_phase_smear_structure (W06-60) — that entry gives the surrounding PREP/SMEAR/SLOWDOWN phase timing template; this entry is specifically about how to draw the SMEAR phase itself once inside it

style_variations.anime: not addressed directly in this source; other sources in this corpus treat a smear as close to a default idiom for a fast strike in this style
style_variations.realistic: the source's own stated basis (long-exposure photography) suggests this technique is meant to read as physically motivated rather than purely stylized, unlike some of this batch's more overtly non-physical smear/impact techniques

cadence_representation: Not represented, for the same reason as `motion_smear_readability`: Cadence has no mesh deformation and no drawn-2D layer, so neither discrete 'doubles' silhouettes nor a flowing streak shape can be produced on a rigid Motor6D rig. A VFX-trail approximation (`ai/vfxspec.js`) is the same substitute already named by that card and by `multiples_vs_smear_for_differently_weighted_fast_motion`, and the same open question about discrete-copy vs. continuous-ribbon trails applies here too.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not measurable in this build: this is a 2D drawing technique with no rig-pose or track-property representation. The one adjacent, already-measurable idea — that blur/spacing density should increase approaching a declared impact/contact marker — is indirectly checkable via `ai/motion.js sampleMotion`'s existing velocity curve against `ai/events.js` markers, the same data `peak_spacing_immediately_before_impact` already relies on.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — no mesh deformation or 2D drawing layer exists to generate a smear with.
failure_modes: drawing smear density uniformly rather than concentrated near the impact point, contradicting what the source's own filmed reference showed
animating a smear on twos rather than ones, reported to read worse
treating doubles and streak-blur as mutually exclusive when the source's own stated best result combines both
roblox_considerations: Same as `motion_smear_readability`: no native mesh deformation, so a `ParticleEmitter`/`Beam` VFX trail is the practical Roblox-native substitute for either construction method, not a rig-pose technique.
performance_implications: None beyond whatever a VFX-trail substitute would cost, outside this entry's scope.
examples: 'notice the blur is increasing towards the impact point — I'm not having a lot of blurs up near where the hammer started swinging from — if you check the reference, that's where I got that from' (video @ 01:22–01:39)

'two strategies I like to use for implementing smear frames — one is doubles ... the next one is blurs ... a bonus third strategy is using both blurs and doubles — this, in my opinion, produces the best effect, I think this is the most natural looking' (video @ 01:39–02:53), confirmed in this session's frames at t=01:45/01:58 (canvas labeled 'DOUBLES' and 'BLURS') and t=02:14 (labeled 'BOTH')
'last tip before we move on ... you want to make smears on ones, animating on ones, they look the best' (video @ 03:20–03:27)
